title: Judge reserves decision in bestselling author Steven Galloway's defamation lawsuit
summary: Steven Galloway is suing a woman and three other defendants over alleged defamatory statements published on social media and elsewhere between 2015 and 2018 regarding claims of sexual assault.

image.caption: Steven Galloway is seen at his former office at the University of British Columbia on March 31, 2014. A judge has reserved a decision on the bestselling author's defamation lawsuit after a trial that lasted over a month. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Steven Galloway is suing a woman and three other defendants over alleged defamatory statements published on social media and elsewhere between 2015 and 2018 regarding claims of sexual assault.
Galloway has sued multiple people after he was accused of sexual assault, with trial taking over a month
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 27, 2026 9:18 PM EST | Last Updated: 40 minutes ago

The B.C. Supreme Court trial has concluded in author Steven Galloway's defamation lawsuit against the woman who accused him of rape, and other defendants, with the judge reserving her decision for a later date.

Justice Neena Sharma told the courtroom that judgments take time, especially when she is hearing other, separate matters, and while she aims to release her written decision within six months, she can't promise she will meet that timeline.

The conclusion of the trial in Vancouver came moments after Sharma dismissed a last-minute application by the lawyer for Galloway's accuser to put the trial over to next year in order to deal with a contempt application involving the woman.

The trial has heard the woman, who cannot be named under a publication ban and did not testify or appear at the trial, violated a court order compelling her to sit for a discovery examination, setting off the contempt application.

The woman's lawyer, Arden Beddoes, had sought to reopen her case shortly before the trial's scheduled conclusion, saying he understood the application was to be dealt with during the trial and he intended to bring evidence related to her risk of suicide in response to it.
The court has heard Galloway is seeking millions of dollars in damages from his accuser and other defendants. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The request to extend the trial until an expert report by a psychiatrist was finished drew a sharp response from Sharma, who questioned Beddoes about why he hadn't raised the issue before or during closing his arguments.
"That would have been the point to say, 'I'm not closing my case, I still have evidence that you need,'" the judge said during the hearing Friday.
Sharma said there was "a way to look at this as the defence changing its position on a fundamental issue at the close of submissions."
Beddoes said he didn't agree that it was a fair characterization.

blocks.text: Galloway denies his accuser's allegations of rape and sexual assault and he is suing the woman only identified as A.B. and three other defendants over alleged defamatory statements published on social media and elsewhere between 2015 and 2018.

Galloway's lawyer, Daniel Burnett, told Sharma he recalled making it clear at the start of the trial they would seek a negative inference to be drawn from A.B.'s absence and file a contempt application related to the discovery examination.
Several settlements
Earlier Friday, Burnett said the court had expressed "reservations" about whether the contempt application should be heard as part of the trial and the issue was left unresolved.
"So, from that point forward, nobody had any business making assumptions about what the court would decide on that point," Burnett said.
Beddoes said it was his client, not Galloway, who would suffer prejudice if she could not bring evidence about her "suicidality" during the trial.

Sharma said A.B.'s non-attendance at trial had always been a "huge issue" in the years-long proceedings after Galloway first filed his lawsuit in 2018.
The judge said she hadn't received first-hand evidence of any kind from A.B. since an affidavit filed in 2021, though her suicide risk was "not a new issue" in the case.
A retired judge hired by the University of B.C., where Galloway was chair of creative writing, found the rape and assault claims against him unsubstantiated.

blocks.text: But Galloway, author of the bestselling novel The Cellist of Sarajevo, was fired from his post. He has testified his career was destroyed.

The trial has heard Galloway is seeking millions of dollars in damages from A.B. and the other defendants, along with an "explicit" finding by the court that the rape and assault allegations are false, should he win his lawsuit.
Several people originally named as defendants in the lawsuit settled with Galloway and issued public apologies before the trial began.
